pages.title: Plan Your Visit
pages.body:
The Museum of Unbuilt Futures stands at 1 Meridian Parade, Marghaven, MB1 9UF — a ten-minute walk from Marghaven Interchange, directly above the tram line it was once predicted would be obsolete by now.

Opening hours

Tuesday – Wednesday, Friday – Sunday10:00 – 18:00
Thursday10:00 – 21:00 (late opening; pay what you wish after 17:00)
MondayClosed (open on bank holidays)

Admission

Adults£9.00
Concessions (students, over-65s)£6.00
Under 12sFree
MembersFree, always
Thursday eveningsPay what you wish, 17:00 – 21:00

Getting here

  • Marghaven Interchange is a ten-minute walk away — leave via the Meridian exit.
  • Tram line 4 stops directly outside at 'Meridian Parade'.
  • Cycle racks at the Parade South entrance; the museum has no visitor car park.
  • Parade South public car park is two streets away (pay and display).

Accessibility

  • Step-free access to all galleries, with lifts at the east and west staircases.
  • Hearing loops in the Lecture Theatre and at both reception desks.
  • Wheelchairs available to borrow from the cloakroom.
  • Quiet Hours: first Sunday of each month, 09:00 – 10:00, with reduced sound and lighting.
  • Registered assistance dogs welcome in all galleries.

Good to know

  • Guided highlights tours run Saturdays and Sundays at 11:00 and 15:00; meet in the entrance hall. Free with admission.
  • The Meridian Café serves breakfast until 11:30 and is licensed from 12:00. The gin mist is available after 17:00 on Thursdays.
  • Photography without flash is welcome. The Cognition Armchair requests that it not be photographed mid-opinion.
  • Coats and umbrellas may be left at the cloakroom; the museum accepts no responsibility for umbrellas that prove, on collection, to have been from another timeline.

Questions we are asked every week

The museum, its exhibits and their histories are lovingly invented. The lessons it draws from them, we would argue, are entirely real.

Most visitors allow two hours for the permanent collection and one exhibition. The Pocket Parliament's shutdown debate, should you choose to hear it in full, adds forty minutes.

Please look with your eyes and read with your hands folded. The one exception is the Megastructure Table in Cities in the Sky, where building something impossible is actively encouraged.

Enthusiastically. Under-12s enter free, the Making Room runs family workshops monthly, and children consistently understand the flying cars before their parents do.

pages.title: About the Museum
pages.body:
The Museum of Unbuilt Futures is a fictional institution with a serious purpose: to collect, study and celebrate the technologies, buildings and schemes that were confidently announced — and never built. We preserve the tomorrows that never happened, so that the ones that did can be seen clearly.

Our mission

Every unbuilt future is a record of hope, arithmetic and ambition colliding. The museum exists to keep that record: the proposals, the prototypes, the brochures with their impossible reflections, and the moments — always documented — when tomorrow was quietly cancelled. We hold that the unbuilt is not the opposite of history. It is history, saved from itself.

A brief institutional timeline

1979Dr. Aurelia Vane founds the museum in a decommissioned planetarium in Marghaven, with eleven objects, one assistant, and no heating.
1984The Servo-Valet 3000 arrives. The 'ironing of the cat' incident is immediately accessioned, per the founder's instruction that 'nothing instructive is uncollectable'.
1993Tomorrow, Cancelled opens as the museum's first full retrospective and has never entirely closed since; it returns this autumn for the sixth time.
2001The register passes 40,000 index cards. Ms. Ines Krieger is appointed Chief Archivist and begins the slow campaign for a second shelf.
2012The Restoration Laboratory is established to conserve objects that were never finished — work the conservators describe as 'restoring them to their original condition'.
2021The Wireframe Reconstruction Programme begins: lost machines re-rendered as luminous wireframe studies, the museum's signature visual language.
2026Three new exhibitions, one domed screening room, and — at last — the second shelf.

The people

Dr. Imogen VaneDirector. Granddaughter of the founder; keeper of the mission.
Prof. Barnaby QuillKeeper of Implausible Devices. Specialist in domestic robotics and overpromised convenience.
Ms. Ines KriegerChief Archivist. Guardian of the MUF register and its 40,000 index cards.
Mr. Tomas ReyesHead of Visitor Experience. Believes wayfinding is a moral obligation.

A note on fiction

The museum, its collection, its staff and its correspondents are inventions, maintained with archival care. Nothing here should be mistaken for a historical claim. Everything here, we hope, might be mistaken for a warning. The site itself — its design, its writing and its imagery — was generated by an AI coding assistant working from a single kickoff prompt; the repository behind it is public.
